title: Group a very large stream of transactions by account id in parallel, using `Collectors.groupingByConcurrent`, and explain how it differs from `groupingBy` on a parallel stream, the requirement for a concurrent map, and the unordered trade-off.
shortTitle: Group a large transaction stream by account in parallel using groupingByConcurrent

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `Collectors.groupingByConcurrent(classifier)` is a concurrent, unordered collector that groups elements into a `ConcurrentMap`. On a parallel stream it lets multiple threads insert into one shared concurrent map simultaneously, avoiding the per-thread-map-then-merge cost that ordinary `groupingBy` incurs in parallel.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Many clerks sort transaction slips into labelled account trays at the same time. groupingByConcurrent gives them one shared set of trays that is safe for everyone to drop slips into at once. Ordinary groupingBy would give each clerk their own trays and then someone must merge all the tray sets at the end.

**One line to remember:** `groupingByConcurrent` fills one shared ConcurrentMap from many threads — faster parallel grouping, but the result is unordered.

sections.s2_technical:
On a sequential stream, `groupingBy` and `groupingByConcurrent` behave similarly. The difference matters in parallel. Ordinary `groupingBy` is a non-concurrent collector, so a parallel stream has each thread build its own partial map and then merges those maps, which costs memory and merge time. `groupingByConcurrent` is a concurrent collector, so all threads insert into a single shared `ConcurrentMap` directly, skipping the merge step.

A worked finance example: `transactions.parallelStream().collect(Collectors.groupingByConcurrent(Txn::getAccountId))` returns a `ConcurrentMap<String, List<Txn>>` grouping all transactions per account, using every core. You can add a downstream collector exactly like groupingBy, for instance `groupingByConcurrent(Txn::getAccountId, counting())`.

The senior nuance is the trade-off: groupingByConcurrent is marked UNORDERED, so within each group the encounter order of elements is not preserved, which is fine for sums or counts but not when order matters. It only helps when the stream is actually parallel and the classifier and downstream are thread-safe. If you need ordered groups or the stream is sequential, plain groupingBy is the right choice. The result type is a ConcurrentMap, so code depending on a specific map type should account for that.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India groups a very large end-of-day stream of transactions by account to compute per-account activity, and it must finish within the batch window by using all CPU cores. With ordinary groupingBy on a parallel stream, each thread builds a separate map and the merge at the end becomes a bottleneck.

This is exactly what groupingByConcurrent solves — all threads insert into one shared ConcurrentMap at once, so there is no costly merge step, and because we only need counts and sums per account, the unordered trade-off is acceptable.

The code defines a `Txn` record, an `ActivityService.countByAccountParallel` method, and a demo.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: ninety thousand transactions spread evenly across three accounts.

Step 1: parallelStream splits the transactions across the fork-join threads.

Step 2: Each thread classifies its transactions by account id and inserts directly into one shared ConcurrentMap, which is safe for concurrent writes.

Step 3: The counting downstream tallies occurrences per account as threads contribute.

Step 4: Because all threads share one map, there is no separate merge of per-thread maps at the end.

Step 5: The final ConcurrentMap shows each of the three accounts with a count of thirty thousand, though the iteration order of accounts is not guaranteed.

```
INFO: ACC-0 txn count = 30000
INFO: ACC-1 txn count = 30000
INFO: ACC-2 txn count = 30000
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
groupingByConcurrent is a concurrent, unordered collector that groups elements into a single shared ConcurrentMap. On a sequential stream it behaves much like groupingBy, but the difference shows up in parallel. Ordinary groupingBy is non-concurrent, so a parallel stream has each thread build its own partial map and then merges them, which costs memory and merge time. groupingByConcurrent lets all threads insert into one shared concurrent map directly, so that merge step disappears and parallel grouping is faster.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India we grouped a very large end-of-day transaction stream by account to compute per-account activity, and it had to finish inside the batch window using every core. I used a parallel stream with groupingByConcurrent on the account id and a counting downstream, which filled one shared ConcurrentMap across all threads and avoided the per-thread-map merge bottleneck.

The senior point I always stress is the trade-off and when not to use it. groupingByConcurrent is marked unordered, so the encounter order of elements within each group is not preserved, which is perfectly fine for counts and sums but wrong when order matters. It only helps when the stream is genuinely parallel and the classifier and downstream are thread-safe, and it returns a ConcurrentMap. For a sequential stream, or when I need ordered groups, I use plain groupingBy instead.
